artiest/gabrieli-consort-en-players-en-p.text:
The Gabrieli Consort & Players is an early-music ensemble founded in 1982 by the English conductor Paul McCreesh, born in 1960. McCreesh began as a cellist and studied at the University of Manchester. He made his name with music of the Renaissance and the Baroque, above all that of Venice. The ensemble takes its name from the Venetian composers Andrea and Giovanni Gabrieli. In 1992 McCreesh and his ensemble made a successful debut at the Proms, where the second half of the concert consisted of music for the coronation of a doge in 1595.

McCreesh is known for his liturgical reconstructions, in which music is presented in the form of a particular service, complete with fitting background sounds such as the ringing of bells. The recording Venetian Coronation, made in 1990, won a Gramophone Award and became the ensemble's breakthrough. A new version followed in 2012. From 1993 he built up a large discography with Deutsche Grammophon, and in 2011 he founded the label Winged Lion. He also conducted modern orchestras and operas by Handel, Gluck and Mozart, and directed festivals in Wrocław in Poland and at Brinkburn in England.

The Gabrielis' music is written for several choirs and brass ensembles, which answer one another across the great space of San Marco in Venice. The ensemble shows how stereo effects already existed in the sixteenth century. Two works return in School of Rock: the Gloria à 16 by Andrea Gabrieli and the Sonata pian' e forte by Giovanni Gabrieli.
artiest/gabrieli-consort-en-players-en-p.listen: Listen to the Sonata pian' e forte by Giovanni Gabrieli. Notice the shift between soft and loud, and how groups of instruments answer one another as if across a great building.

artiest/gaia-sokoli.text:
Gaia Sokoli is a pianist who became known through a recording with a remarkable story behind it. In May 2020 she was the first to record the Ostersonate under the name of Fanny Hensel, also known as Fanny Mendelssohn. The recording was released in 2021 by Piano Classics on the album Piano Sonatas.

The sonata in A major dates from 1828. The manuscript was found in France in 1970 and bore the signature F. Mendelssohn. It was therefore assumed to be by Felix Mendelssohn, and Éric Heidsieck recorded it in 1972 under his name. In 2010 Angela Mace Christian established that the handwriting was Fanny's own and that the pages had been cut from her composition book. In 2012 the piece was first heard under her name, played by Andrea Lam.

The sonata depicts the Passion of Christ. The second movement contains a church fugue, and the finale gives musical form to the moment when the veil of the temple is torn. The piece ends with a fantasia on the chorale Christe, du Lamm Gottes. With her recording, the work was for the first time placed under the name of its own composer.
artiest/gaia-sokoli.listen: Listen to the Ostersonate in the recording by Gaia Sokoli and pay attention to the ending, where the chorale Christe, du Lamm Gottes sounds. Try to hear where the music passes from the fantasia into the chorale.

artiest/galliano.text:
Galliano is an acid jazz group from London, active from 1988 to 1997 and together again since 2023. They were the first to record for the label Acid Jazz, run by Eddie Piller and Gilles Peterson, and then the first to sign to Peterson's new label Talkin' Loud. Robert Gallagher, who called himself Roberto Galliano, was joined by Constantine Weir and the percussionist Crispin Robinson. The trio performed spoken-word pieces influenced by the Last Poets. Michael Snaith joined when the trio became a band so that it could tour.

The first single was Frederick Lies Still from June 1988, an adaptation of Freddie's Dead by Curtis Mayfield and also the first release on Acid Jazz. The debut album In Pursuit of the 13th Note appeared in 1991, produced by Chris Bangs, with Roy Ayers as a guest. A Joyful Noise Unto the Creator followed in 1992 and The Plot Thickens in 1994. That last album reached number eight in the UK albums chart and yielded two UK top 40 singles: Long Time Gone, a cover of David Crosby, and Twyford Down, a comment on the protests against road building. In 1994 the band played at the Glastonbury Festival, and again in 1995. In 1997 the group split up after a farewell show in Camden.

Galliano linked acid jazz with the spoken word. Valerie Etienne worked on all of their albums, and the group also had a dancer, Steve Ameedee. They belong to the British acid jazz movement of the 1990s. In 2024 they again played a sold-out show at Shepherd's Bush Empire.
artiest/galliano.listen: Listen to Long Time Gone from 1994 and notice the vocals and the band. If you can, compare it with David Crosby's original.

artiest/gamelan-of-the-yogyakarta-royal-.text:
The gamelan of the royal palace of Yogyakarta is the ensemble that plays the court music of Central Java. Gamelan itself is the traditional ensemble music of the Javanese, Sundanese and Balinese in Indonesia and consists mainly of percussion instruments. The word comes from the Javanese gamel, which refers to playing percussion or striking with a mallet. In 2014 gamelan traditions were recognised as National Intangible Cultural Heritage of Indonesia, and in 2021 UNESCO added gamelan to the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The sound comes from metal instruments such as gongs, metallophones and small gong chimes, supplemented by drums and often by strings, flute and voice. The ensemble has no conductor in the Western sense: a drummer or another leading instrument signals the changes. The pieces have fixed forms, of which the ladrang is one, and are played in one of two tuning systems, pelog or slendro, in a particular pathet, a kind of choice of mode. Ladrang Liwung in pelog pathet barang follows such a form.

For anyone who listens to pop music, gamelan matters because it shows what an interplay of repeated cycles sounds like, with layers that each run at their own tempo. These sounds later inspired Western composers and pop musicians. The palace tradition of Yogyakarta is regarded as one of the forms in which this music has been preserved in its purest state.
artiest/gamelan-of-the-yogyakarta-royal-.listen: Listen to Ladrang Liwung, and first listen for the great gong, which sounds only now and then. Then try to hear how the higher instruments move faster around that slow structure.

artiest/gamelan-pura-paku-alaman.text:
The gamelan of the Pura Paku Alaman is the court orchestra of the court of Paku Alaman in Yogyakarta, on Java in Indonesia. It is a heirloom: the instruments were made in 1755 for Paku Alam I. The gamelan consists of two halves. The sléndro half is called Kyai Pengawé Sari, which means Lord Invitation to Beauty. The pélog half is called Kyai Telaga Muntjar, Lord Lake and Fountain. Sléndro and pélog are the two tunings of the Javanese gamelan.

The ethnomusicologist Robert E. Brown recorded the orchestra on 10 January 1971 in the reception hall of the court, with the permission of Paku Alam VIII, for a radio broadcast in honour of his birthday. The recording was released on LP that same year under the title Javanese Court Gamelan and appeared on CD in 1991. In 2003 it was reissued as Java: Court Gamelan. K.R.T. Wasitodiningrat led the orchestra, and the singers Nyi Djiworetno, Niken Larasati and Nyi Tasri sang along. The sounds of sparrows nesting in the hall can be heard on the recording and are considered normal.

The recording became known worldwide because Ketawang Puspawarna was included on the Voyager Golden Record, the disc that travelled into space with the Voyager probes. In 1972 the album was nominated for a Grammy for best ethnic or traditional folk recording.
artiest/gamelan-pura-paku-alaman.listen: Listen to Ketawang Puspawarna, the piece on the Voyager Golden Record, and notice the singers among the instruments. Can you also hear the sounds of the hall itself?

artiest/gamelan-pura-paku-alaman-k-r-t-w.text:
In the course, the gamelan of the Paku Alaman palace in Yogyakarta is led by K.R.T. Wasitodipuro, a name that also appears in the sources as Tjokrowasito, Wasitodiningrat and Notoprojo. He was born on 17 March 1909 in Yogyakarta and died on 30 August 2007. His official name changed several times, in keeping with the honorific titles he received during his life. He was regarded as one of the most highly esteemed performers of Javanese gamelan.

Wasitodipuro grew up in the palace. At the age of five he began learning gamelan from his legal father, R.W. Padmowinangum, who led the palace orchestra. He also played in other famous groups, such as Daya Pradangga, and from 1934 he was musical director of gamelan at the radio station MAVRO. In 1962 he took over from his father as leader of the gamelan of Pura Pakualaman. The style of this palace had elements of both the court of the sultan of Yogyakarta and that of the sunan in Solo. In 2004 he received the Nugraha Bhakti Musik Indonesia Award.

Ketawang Puspawarna from 1971 is a piece from that court tradition. A ketawang is a fixed, fairly short form in Javanese gamelan music, in which gong strokes mark the cycle. He is regarded as one of the important custodians of classical Javanese court music.
artiest/gamelan-pura-paku-alaman-k-r-t-w.listen: Listen to Ketawang Puspawarna and try to follow the recurring gong strokes as markers of a cycle. Notice how the melody in the higher-sounding instruments keeps moving around that fixed structure.

artiest/gang-of-four.text:
Gang of Four is an English post-punk band, formed in Leeds in 1976. The original line-up consisted of singer Jon King, guitarist Andy Gill, drummer Hugo Burnham and bassist Dave Wolfson, who was replaced by Dave Allen after two gigs. The band drew on the Frankfurt School of social critique and on punk. The name came from Andy Corrigan of the Mekons, who saw a newspaper headline about the Chinese Gang of Four.

The first single, Damaged Goods, with (Love Like) Anthrax and Armalite Rifle, was recorded in June 1978 and released on 10 December 1978 on the label Fast Product. It was a number 1 in the indie chart and a favourite of the radio presenter John Peel. The debut album Entertainment! followed in 1979, then Solid Gold in 1981, Songs of the Free in 1982 and Hard in 1983. The group later went through many different line-ups and released, among others, Return the Gift in 2005 and Happy Now in 2019.

The music is a stark mix of punk rock, funk and dub, with lyrics about the social and political problems of the time. Sharp, angular guitar sounds and a tightly playing rhythm section form the core. Gang of Four is considered one of the most important groups of post-punk. Entertainment! ranks high on Rolling Stone's list of the best albums, and many later bands built on this combination of politics and danceable rhythms.
artiest/gang-of-four.listen: Listen to Damaged Goods and follow the bass and the drums separately: can you hear how they lay down a funky, driving rhythm? Then notice the sharp, angular guitar playing on top of it.

artiest/gang-starr.text:
Gang Starr was an American hip hop duo, made up of the rapper Guru from Boston and the producer DJ Premier from Houston. The name already existed: the first group was formed at Morehouse College by three friends from Boston, Guru, Big Shug and DJ Suave D. After a first and a second split, only Guru remained. He invited DJ Premier, who was then still called Waxmaster C, to move to Brooklyn. In 1989 their first single Words I Manifest appeared, together with the album No More Mr. Nice Guy.

In 1990 the group signed to Chrysalis, which offered the duo a great deal of artistic freedom and worldwide distribution. Step in the Arena followed, then Daily Operation in 1992, Hard to Earn in 1994 and Moment of Truth in 1998. Among their best-known songs are Mass Appeal, Take It Personal, Full Clip and Above the Clouds. Jazz Thing was on the soundtrack of Spike Lee's Mo' Better Blues, and Battle on that of 8 Mile.

Gang Starr is regarded as one of the pioneers of jazz rap in the golden age of hip hop and helped shape the hardcore New York hip hop sound. The duo had a fixed division of labour: Premier made the music, Guru rapped. At the end of 2002 Premier returned to the United States, and in 2019 one more album appeared, One of the Best Yet.
artiest/gang-starr.listen: Listen to Jazz Thing and notice how jazz and hip hop come together in a single track. Try to hear what the producer does and what the rapper says over it.

artiest/gary-brooker.text:
Gary Brooker was born in 1945 in Hackney, in East London. His father was a professional musician who played steel guitar. As a child Gary learned piano, cornet and trombone. The family moved to Southend-on-Sea, where his father died when Gary was eleven. He began a degree in zoology and botany but gave it up to become a musician. In 1962 he formed The Paramounts with the guitarist Robin Trower, an R&B band that even counted The Rolling Stones among its fans.

In 1966 Brooker started the band Procol Harum with the lyricist Keith Reid. A year later A Whiter Shade of Pale became a worldwide hit, followed by Homburg. In the early years Brooker, the organist Matthew Fisher and Trower together shaped the music. After Fisher and Trower left, Brooker was clearly the leader. He later began a solo career with No More Fear of Flying (1979), played in Eric Clapton's band and sang Limelight by The Alan Parsons Project. He also played on albums by George Harrison, including All Things Must Pass.

The sound of Procol Harum revolved around Brooker's melancholy voice and his sensitive, versatile piano playing, alongside the Hammond organ. For a long time only Brooker was credited as the composer of A Whiter Shade of Pale. In 2005 Matthew Fisher went to court, because he felt he had co-written the music. He won in 2006 and was awarded forty per cent of the composer's share. Brooker continued to tour with Procol Harum until 2019 and died in 2022.
artiest/gary-brooker.listen: Listen to A Whiter Shade of Pale and notice the two keyboard players. Hear how Matthew Fisher's Hammond organ plays the famous melody, while the piano and Gary Brooker's voice carry the song.

artiest/gary-burton.text:
Gary Burton is an American vibraphonist, composer and teacher, born on 23 January 1943 in Anderson, Indiana. He taught himself to play marimba and vibraphone, began piano lessons at the age of sixteen, and names the pianist Bill Evans as an inspiration for his approach. He studied briefly at the Berklee College of Music in Boston and, as a teenager in Nashville, made recordings with, among others, Hank Garland and Chet Atkins. He then toured with George Shearing, for whom he wrote the album Out of the Woods, and from 1964 to 1966 played with the saxophonist Stan Getz.

In 1967 Burton formed the Gary Burton Quartet with the guitarist Larry Coryell, the drummer Roy Haynes and the bassist Steve Swallow. The first album, Duster, combined jazz, country and rock, before the fusion of the 1970s had broken loose. Records such as The Time Machine from 1966 also pointed in that direction. In 1968 he became the youngest ever DownBeat Jazzman of the Year, and in 1972 he won his first Grammy. In 1973 he began a collaboration with the pianist Chick Corea that lasted forty years and produced Crystal Silence. Together they made eight Grammy-winning albums and brought the jazz duo to wider attention as a form.

Burton developed his own way of holding four mallets, the Burton grip, with which he played the vibraphone like a piano. From 1971 to 2004 he taught at Berklee, in his last years as vice president. In 2017 he stopped performing after a farewell tour with Makoto Ozone.
artiest/gary-burton.listen: Listen to Crystal Silence, the duo with Chick Corea, and notice how the vibraphone and the piano share chords and melody. Try to hear who plays the melody and who accompanies.

artiest/gary-haisman.text:
Gary Haisman was an English singer and a well-known figure of the London acid house scene. He was born on 29 January 1958 and died on 28 November 2018. Before he could be heard on a record, he worked as a club promoter and was a striking face and dancer in the London clubs. He organised nights such as Raid at various clubs, including Shoom, and by the end of the 1980s was one of the best-known names of the acid house scene. He was also the PR manager of Spectrum, London's first acid house club, and was part of the editorial team of the fanzine Boys Own, together with Terry Farley and Andrew Weatherall.

His musical contribution was the double single We Call It Acieed and Trance Dance. It was the first of four consecutive number 1 hits for D Mob on Billboard's US dance chart in 1989 and appeared on the album A Little Bit of This, a Little Bit of That. Haisman is also the originator of the expression It's all gone Pete Tong, which later inspired the title of a dance music film and was adopted by Pete Tong himself at his nights in Ibiza.

Haisman lived in Spain for years, developed a deep vein thrombosis there and came close to death. Later he returned to the United Kingdom and renewed contact with people from the acid house scene. His name shows that acid house was not just a sound but also a community of club makers and dancers.
artiest/gary-haisman.listen: Listen to We Call It Acieed by D Mob and notice the vocals and the rhythm. The track opens the series of dance hits by D Mob from 1989.

artiest/gary-mcfarland.text:
Gary McFarland was an American composer, arranger, conductor, vibraphonist and singer. He was born on 23 October 1933 in Los Angeles and moved at the age of fifteen to Grants Pass in Oregon. He died on 2 November 1971 in New York, aged 38. In the 1960s he recorded for the jazz labels Verve and Impulse!. He became known through his work with Bill Evans, Gerry Mulligan, Johnny Hodges, John Lewis, Stan Getz, Bob Brookmeyer and Anita O'Day.

McFarland's reputation rests above all on his arrangements for orchestral jazz. DownBeat called him an important contributor to that genre, and a reviewer of a documentary described him as one of the busiest arrangers on the New York jazz circuit of the 1960s. His rise coincided with that of bossa nova, and he was good at translating that form into orchestral settings. Albums from that time include Point of Departure from 1964, Soft Samba from 1965, Profiles from 1966, The In Sound from 1966, The October Suite from 1967 and Today from 1969. For film he wrote the music for Eye of the Devil from 1966 and Who Killed Mary What's 'Er Name? from 1971.

At the end of the 1960s he moved away from jazz towards an often wistful instrumental pop. He also produced other people's recordings on his own label Skye Records, which he ran with Norman Schwartz, Gábor Szabó and Cal Tjader until it went bankrupt in 1970. He also worked on the soft rock album Genesis by the sisters Wendy and Bonnie Flower.
artiest/gary-mcfarland.listen: Listen to a track from Soft Samba and notice how a Brazilian rhythm has been translated into jazz. Try to hear what the arrangement adds.

artiest/gary-numan.text:
Gary Numan's real name is Gary Webb, and he was born in 1958 in Hammersmith, in West London. His father was a bus driver at Heathrow airport. At fifteen he was given a Gibson Les Paul guitar, and through advertisements in Melody Maker he played in several small bands. One of them became Tubeway Army, with Paul Gardiner on bass. He took his surname Numan from a plumber's advertisement in the Yellow Pages.

Tubeway Army began in 1978 as a punk band. During the recording of the first album Numan found a Moog synthesizer that had been left behind in the studio, and so began the move to an electronic sound. In 1979 Are 'Friends' Electric? spent four weeks at number 1 in Britain, and the album Replicas also went to the top. That same year he continued under his own name. The Pleasure Principle (1979) and the single Cars both went to number 1, and Cars was also a hit in America. With Telekon (1980) he had his third number 1 album. After that his success declined, although he kept a loyal group of fans.

Numan is regarded as a pioneer of electronic pop music. The Pleasure Principle was a rock record without guitars: he ran his synthesizers through effects units, which gave a distorted, metallic sound. To this came his distinctive voice, his love of dark science fiction and his androgynous, robot-like appearance. He was a model for later bands such as Depeche Mode, Nine Inch Nails and Goldfrapp.
artiest/gary-numan.listen: Listen to Are 'Friends' Electric? by Tubeway Army and notice the heavy synthesizer parts. Hear how they sound like distorted guitar riffs, and how cool and detached Numan sounds as he sings above them.

artiest/gary-peacock.text: The bassist Gary Peacock grew up in Idaho and began as a pianist. In the 1960s he played in New York with Bill Evans, Paul Bley and Albert Ayler, with whom he recorded Spiritual Unity (1964). He then stopped playing music for a time, lived in Japan and studied Zen Buddhism and biology. In 1977 he recorded Tales of Another for ECM, with Keith Jarrett and Jack DeJohnette. From that session grew, in 1983, the Standards Trio, which lasted thirty years. Peacock's playing is melodic and open, with a great deal of space.
artiest/gary-peacock.listen: Hear how the bass plays melodies between the piano and the drums.

artiest/gato-barbieri.text:
Gato Barbieri was an Argentine jazz saxophonist, born on 28 November 1932 in Rosario and died on 2 April 2016 in New York. His nickname Gato means cat in Spanish. He grew up in a musical family and began making music after hearing Charlie Parker's Now's the Time. He played clarinet and later alto sax, including with the Argentine pianist Lalo Schifrin at the end of the 1950s. In the early 1960s he worked in Rome with the trumpeter Don Cherry. Influenced by the late recordings of John Coltrane and by Albert Ayler and Pharoah Sanders, he developed the warm, raw tone for which he became known.

At the end of the 1960s he brought South American music into his playing and took part in projects such as Charlie Haden's Liberation Music Orchestra and Carla Bley's Escalator over the Hill. He wrote the film score for Bernardo Bertolucci's Last Tango in Paris from 1972, for which he won a Grammy and was given a record contract with Impulse!. The series Chapter One to Chapter Four followed. In the mid-1970s he signed to A&M and his music moved towards soul jazz and jazz pop. The album Caliente! from 1976, produced by Herb Alpert, contains his best-known song, an adaptation of Europa by Carlos Santana.

After the death of his wife Michelle in 1995 he did not perform for a time. At the end of the 1990s he returned, among other things with the album Qué Pasa from 1997, which moved more towards smooth jazz. He was the inspiration for the character Zoot in the band Dr. Teeth and the Electric Mayhem from The Muppets.
artiest/gato-barbieri.listen: Listen to his version of Europa by Carlos Santana on Caliente! and notice the warm, raw tone of the tenor saxophone. Try to hear how the saxophone takes over the melody of a rock song.

artiest/gaylord-carter.text:
Gaylord Carter was born in 1905 in Wiesbaden, the son of a church organist and a singing teacher. The family moved to Wichita in Kansas, where his father opened a music conservatory. Gaylord sang in a church choir as a boy and from the age of ten played the organ in a church. When the Jazz Age began, he tried jazz on the church organ, until the minister reprimanded him. At fourteen he was already playing in a local cinema, where he accompanied silent films for children's matinees.

In 1922 the family moved to Los Angeles. He played piano and later organ in a cinema and studied at UCLA. In 1926 he accompanied a Harold Lloyd film in Inglewood, where a member of Lloyd's staff heard him. Lloyd recommended him to Sid Grauman, who offered the twenty-one-year-old Carter a permanent job as organist in his picture palace in downtown Los Angeles. In this way he grew into one of the best-known organists of the silent film.

Later Carter wrote a great deal of film music that was added to silent films released on video and record. Records such as The Golden Age Of Silent Movies from 1962 preserve that sound. He died in 2000. The cinema organ imitates a whole orchestra with its stops and makes sounds such as bells and percussion. In School of Rock he is mentioned in connection with music for The Phantom of the Opera from 1925 and Intolerance from 1916, films in which the music had to carry the whole story.
artiest/gaylord-carter.listen: Listen to Gaylord Carter playing for The Phantom of the Opera. Notice how the organ sets the tension: low, menacing sounds at moments of danger and fast, light ones in the action.

artiest/gazebo.text:
Gazebo is the stage name of Paul Mazzolini, an Italian singer, songwriter and producer, born on 18 February 1960 in Beirut. His father worked there as a diplomat at the Italian embassy, and his mother was American. The family later lived in Jordan, Denmark and France. Mazzolini learned to speak Danish in Denmark and worked as a guitarist in London. In 1983 he graduated in French literature. He chose his name after the garden pavilion of that name, because he thought it sounded catchy.

Gazebo became known in the 1980s with Italo disco. His debut single Masterpiece appeared in 1982 and reached number two in Italy. In 1983 came I Like Chopin, which reached number 1 in Italy, Germany, Spain, Austria, Switzerland and, in total, in more than fifteen countries. That same year Lunatic made the top ten in several European, Asian and Latin American countries. His work from that period was produced by Pierluigi Giombini, with whom he also wrote Dolce Vita for the singer Ryan Paris. His albums include Gazebo from 1983, Telephone Mama from 1984, Univision from 1987 and The Rainbow Tales from 1988.

In 1997 he started his own label, Softworks. He continues to perform, works on new albums and produces for other artists. In 2014 he appeared in the comedy Sexy Shop. Gazebo stands for the electronic, melodic dance pop of Italy in the early 1980s, which was played all over Europe.
artiest/gazebo.listen: Listen to I Like Chopin and notice the electronic sounds and the memorable melodic line. Try to hear how the track puts a classical composer into a disco song.

artiest/geike.text:
Geike Arnaert is a Belgian singer, born in 1979 in Poperinge. She grew up in Westouter, close to the French border, and at the age of nine already took part in a talent contest in her village. In 1997 she auditioned for Hooverphonic, the band of Alex Callier and Raymond Geerts. She was not yet eighteen when she went on tour with the group. With her clear, somewhat airy voice she became the face of Hooverphonic, who broke through in 2000 with Mad About You from the album The Magnificent Tree.

At the end of 2008 she left the band to go her own way. She felt that her role was limited to singing, while she had artistic ideas of her own. With Spinvis she made music for the Flemish film Adem, under the name Dorléac, and in 2011 she released her first solo album under the name Geike, For the Beauty of Confusion. In 2019 came Lost in Time, made with Joost Zweegers. She also sang with Bobbejaan Schoepen, Tom Helsen and Ozark Henry.

Her biggest hit came in 2017, when she recorded Zoutelande with the Dutch band BLØF. The song reached number 1 in the Netherlands and Flanders and grew into one of the biggest Dutch-language hits ever. In this way a Flemish voice carried a song from Zeeland across the whole language area. In 2020 she returned to Hooverphonic, with whom she represented Belgium at the Eurovision Song Contest in 2021.
artiest/geike.listen: Listen to Zoutelande and notice how the voice of Geike Arnaert and that of BLØF's singer alternate and come together in the chorus. Can you hear that she sings with a Flemish accent?

artiest/geinoh-yamashirogumi.text:
Geinoh Yamashirogumi is a Japanese music collective founded on 19 January 1974 by Tsutomu Ōhashi. The group consists of hundreds of people from a wide range of professions. The name is derived from Ōhashi's pseudonym Shoji Yamashiro and means roughly Yamashiro Performing Arts Collective. Ōhashi was inspired by a postwar group from the 1950s that lived as a commune.

The collective is known for two things: recreating folk music from all over the world, and music that combines traditional and modern elements. For instance, they made an electronic recreation of Indonesian gamelan, because digital MIDI synthesizers could not handle the tuning of that system. Their records from the 1970s and 1980s carry Japanese titles. In 1988 they made the music for the anime film Akira, including Kaneda.

The music of Akira sounds like a blend of choral singing, percussion and electronic sounds, and is one of the best-known examples of how a large collective could forge traditional sounds into a contemporary film score. Geinoh Yamashirogumi shows that pop music and film could also absorb ideas from far outside Europe and America, and that electronics did not have to sound cold.
artiest/geinoh-yamashirogumi.listen: Listen to Kaneda and notice the communal singing and the percussion that together give a ritual feeling. Try to hear which sounds seem to come from a tradition and which are electronic.

artiest/gene-austin.text:
Gene Austin, born Lemeul Eugene Lucas on 24 June 1900 in Gainesville, Texas, was an American singer and songwriter and one of the first crooners. He took the name of his stepfather and grew up in Minden, Louisiana. At fifteen he ran away from home, sang for the first time in a vaudeville show in Houston and joined the army. After his return in 1919 he lived in Baltimore, where he played piano and sang in bars and put together a vaudeville act. In 1924 he was in New York's Tin Pan Alley. He died on 24 January 1972.

His great years were the late 1920s. Bye Bye Blackbird from 1926 made that year's top twenty. My Blue Heaven spent 26 weeks in the charts in 1928, thirteen of them at number 1, and was the best-selling record of all time until Bing Crosby's White Christmas. Ramona and Carolina Moon followed, both also at number 1. At the height of his career Austin demanded that only the pianist Fats Waller accompany him on his records. The Depression of the 1930s hit the record industry and with it his career.

Austin never learned to read music, but wrote more than a hundred songs. When My Sugar Walks Down the Street and The Lonesome Road became jazz and pop standards, and The Lonesome Road has been recorded by dozens of artists, from Bing Crosby to Frank Sinatra. He appeared in films such as Belle of the Nineties and My Little Chickadee and had a radio series from 1932 to 1934. In this way he helped to shape the crooning sound.
artiest/gene-austin.listen: Listen to My Blue Heaven and notice the way of singing. Austin is regarded as one of the first crooners: can you hear how the voice moves calmly through the song, without straining?

artiest/gene-kelly.text:
Gene Kelly, in full Eugene Curran Kelly, was an American dancer, actor, singer, director and choreographer. He was born on 23 August 1912 in Pittsburgh and died on 2 February 1996. He grew up as one of five children. As a boy he was sporty and could hold his own in a fight, and only later did he choose dance. He first studied journalism, but after the stock market crash of 1929 he chose a different path.

His film debut was For Me and My Gal in 1942, with Judy Garland. Later came, among others, Anchors Aweigh in 1945, for which he received an Oscar nomination, The Pirate in 1948, An American in Paris in 1951, which won the Oscar for best picture, and Summer Stock in 1950. Singin' in the Rain from 1952 he directed and choreographed together with Stanley Donen. In the 1960s he went on directing, including Hello, Dolly! in 1969.

Kelly was known for his energetic, athletic style of dance. He wanted to create a new American dance form for the general public, which he called dance for the common man. His innovations changed the Hollywood musical, and he is praised for having made the form of ballet acceptable to a film audience almost single-handedly. Through his dancing, the title song of Singin' in the Rain became an image that many people associate with the film.
artiest/gene-kelly.listen: Listen to Singin' in the Rain and notice how his voice sounds light-footed and cheerful, with a rhythm that almost invites you to dance by itself. Can you hear how the orchestra seems to follow his steps?

artiest/gene-krupa.text: The drummer Gene Krupa came from Chicago and became, in the swing years, the first drummer to be seen as a star. In 1927 he was one of the first to have the bass drum heard on a record. He played with Benny Goodman from 1934; his tom-toms in Sing, Sing, Sing made the drummer the centre of the stage. In 1938 he started his own big band, in which, from 1941, the singer Anita O'Day and the trumpeter Roy Eldridge performed. Eldridge was one of the first Black musicians to play regularly in a white big band. Krupa's playing was loud and theatrical, and he made the drum solo popular with a wide audience.
artiest/gene-krupa.listen: Follow the tom-toms: here the drums are not at the back but at the front.

artiest/gene-vincent.text:
Gene Vincent's real name was Vincent Eugene Craddock, and he was born in 1935 in Norfolk, Virginia. He grew up with country, rhythm and blues and gospel, and received his first guitar at the age of twelve. At seventeen he joined the US Navy. In 1955 his left leg was shattered in a motorcycle accident. He refused an amputation, but was left with a limp and a great deal of pain, and from then on wore a steel brace on his leg.

After his discharge from the navy he started the band Gene Vincent and His Blue Caps in Norfolk, with Cliff Gallup on lead guitar. In 1956 he wrote Be-Bop-a-Lula. The song was actually the B-side of his first single for Capitol, but radio stations played precisely this song, and it became a big hit. Race with the Devil, Bluejean Bop and Lotta Lovin' followed, among others. In the film The Girl Can't Help It he played Be-Bop-a-Lula with his band. In 1960 he was seriously injured in England in the car crash in which his friend Eddie Cochran was killed.

Vincent was one of the pioneers of rockabilly, a blend of country and rhythm and blues. In America his success was short-lived, but in England he was a bigger star and had eight top 40 hits between 1956 and 1961. There he became a hero of the rockers. He died in 1971 and was later inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/gene-vincent.listen: Listen to Be-Bop-a-Lula and notice the soft, breathy way in which Vincent sings the title words. Then hear how Cliff Gallup's guitar plays fiercely and fast in the solos between the verses.

artiest/gene-vincent-en-his-blue-caps.text:
Gene Vincent, born Vincent Eugene Craddock on 11 February 1935 in Norfolk, Virginia, was an American rock 'n' roll musician who helped shape rockabilly. His musical influences were country, rhythm and blues and gospel. In 1952, at seventeen, he left school and joined the navy, where he planned a career. On 4 July 1955 his left leg was broken in a motorcycle accident. He refused amputation, but was left with a limp and pain.

With his backing band the Blue Caps he reached the American top ten in 1956 with Be-Bop-A-Lula. That song is regarded as an important early example of rockabilly. His hit career was short, but his records from those years, such as Bluejean Bop! in 1956, Gene Vincent and the Blue Caps in 1957 and Gene Vincent Rocks! & The Blue Caps Roll in 1958, remained influential. He was later inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and the Rockabilly Hall of Fame, and was also known as the Screaming End. He died on 12 October 1971.

The music combines a bouncing rhythm section with a sharp electric guitar and a voice that moves back and forth between whispering and screaming. Gene Vincent brought out a dark, rebellious side of early rock 'n' roll. He belongs to the pioneers of a style on which many later guitar bands built.
artiest/gene-vincent-en-his-blue-caps.listen: Listen to Be-Bop-A-Lula and notice the echo on the voice and the rhythm, which starts quietly and yet drives forward. Can you hear how the voice sometimes almost whispers and then lets rip?

artiest/general-levy.text:
General Levy, in full Paul Scott Levy, is an English raggamuffin deejay, born on 28 April 1971 in Park Royal in London. He has Trinidadian roots. He grew up in Harlesden and Wembley, in north-west London, and fell under the spell of dancehall there. He collected dancehall cassettes and performed at sound systems such as Java and Tippertone Sound. His first major releases came on the independent label Fashion Records, which struck a distribution deal with London Records for the reissues.

His best-known song is Incredible, which he recorded with M-Beat. A remixed version reached number eight in the UK chart in 1994. The song was heard in the film Ali G Indahouse and in a TV campaign for Honda. His albums include Double Trouble from 1991, The Wickeder General from 1992 and Wickedness Increase from 1993. He also worked with Suggs of Madness and with the dub producer Joe Ariwa, and he can be heard on Only God Can Judge Me by Mark Morrison.

General Levy sings and toasts in a fast, sharp style above heavy basslines, and is often hired by drum and bass DJs for studio tracks. He belongs to the generation of British deejays who brought dancehall and ragga together with jungle and drum and bass. Incredible is one of the best-known examples of this, and shows how London club music in the 1990s combined reggae language, fast breakbeats and pop.
artiest/general-levy.listen: Listen to Incredible and notice the fast, rattling toasting above a driving breakbeat. Which words or sounds stay with you, and how heavy does the bass sound underneath?

artiest/genesis.text:
Genesis began in 1967 at Charterhouse School in Godalming, a boarding school in Surrey. The founders were pupils: Tony Banks, Mike Rutherford, Peter Gabriel, Anthony Phillips and the drummer Chris Stewart. They got their name from Jonathan King, a former pupil who worked as an impresario and had their debut album From Genesis to Revelation, from 1969, recorded. The group then chose its own path at Charisma Records, with Trespass in 1970 as a first step towards progressive rock. With Phil Collins and Steve Hackett added, the line-up of Nursery Cryme and Foxtrot came about.

In the 1970s Genesis were among the pioneers of progressive rock. Their live shows became famous for Gabriel's theatrical costumes and performances. Selling England by the Pound from 1973 brought the first British hit, I Know What I Like (In Your Wardrobe). After the concept double album The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, Gabriel left the band. Collins took over the vocals, and after Hackett's departure a trio remained: Banks, Rutherford and Collins.

With ...And Then There Were Three... (1978) came the first big hit, Follow You Follow Me. On Duke, Abacab, Genesis and Invisible Touch the band sounded more and more like a pop group, and that success lasted until We Can't Dance in 1991. In 1996 Collins left, and Ray Wilson sang on the last studio album, Calling All Stations. The course mentions Genesis in connection with the design agency Hipgnosis, which also made sleeves for this band. That shows how closely image and music went together in the 1970s.
artiest/genesis.listen: Listen to Follow You Follow Me. Notice how short and poppy this song is, and think how different the long songs from the Gabriel period must have sounded.

artiest/geoff-barrow.text:
Geoff Barrow is an English producer, composer and DJ, born on 9 December 1971 in Walton in Gordano. At the age of eleven he moved with his mother to Portishead, the small town near Bristol from which he would later take his band's name. He played drums, spun records in hip hop groups and in 1989 got a job as tape operator at Coach House Studios. In 1991 he helped out on Massive Attack's Blue Lines, and was given studio time to record ideas of his own. During a break he met Beth Gibbons. Together they formed Portishead, later joined by Adrian Utley. Their debut album Dummy appeared in 1994. Barrow said he wanted to make music that was gripping, real songs with real life in them.

Besides Portishead he worked as a remixer for, among others, Primal Scream, Paul Weller and Depeche Mode, and produced a track for Tricky. With Utley he produced The Coral's The Invisible Invasion in 2005. In 2001 he founded the label Invada, and later formed the groups Beak and Quakers. With Beak he played on Anika's debut album in 2010.

Since 2013 he has written film music with Ben Salisbury, beginning with Alex Garland's Ex Machina. Annihilation followed in 2018, the series Devs in 2020, Men in 2022 and Civil War in 2024. They also made music for the Black Mirror episode Men Against Fire and for Archive 81. Barrow shows how the Bristol scene of the 1990s carried on into film and television.
artiest/geoff-barrow.listen: Listen to an excerpt from the music for Ex Machina and notice how the music carries the atmosphere of the film. Ask yourself what feeling the music evokes without the images.

artiest/geoff-downes.text:
Geoff Downes is an English keyboard player, born on 25 August 1952 in Stockport. His father was a church organist and his mother a pianist. He played in local bands, studied at the Leeds College of Music and then moved to London, where he did session work and wrote advertising jingles. In the mid-1970s he played, among others, with She's French and on Gary Boyle's Isotope. In 1976 he met Trevor Horn, with whom in 1978 he recorded the album Star to Star in the short-lived Chromium, together with Anne Dudley and Hans Zimmer.

In 1977 he formed the Buggles with Horn. Their album The Age of Plastic from 1980 contained Video Killed the Radio Star, the first number 1 for Island Records in the United Kingdom. In May 1980 Downes moved with Horn to Yes, where they recorded Drama. After the break-up of Yes in 1981 he helped Horn with the second Buggles album Adventures in Modern Recording and formed Asia with Steve Howe. He left Asia in 1986, returned in 1990 and made solo albums including The Light Program from 1987 and Vox Humana from 1992. He also produced for Mike Oldfield and the Thompson Twins.

In 2006 he brought the original line-up of Asia back together, and in 2011 he rejoined Yes. He entered the Guinness Book of Records by playing 28 keyboards in a single performance. He is one of the keyboard players who linked new wave and progressive rock.
artiest/geoff-downes.listen: Listen to Video Killed the Radio Star by the Buggles and notice the keyboards and the vocals. Ask yourself what role the keyboards play here.

artiest/geoff-wilkinson.text:
Geoff Wilkinson is a London producer who founded the British jazz rap group Us3 in 1992. In the early 1990s he made two recordings under that name. The first was Where Will We Be in the 21st Century from 1990, a limited-edition white-label twelve-inch. With it he attracted the attention of the independent label Ninja Tune, which in 1991 resulted in The Band Played The Boogie by NW1, with the British rapper Born 2 B.

For Us3, Wilkinson worked with the producer Mel Simpson. One of the demos from March 1992 was Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia), with the British trumpeter Gerard Presencer. The track used a sample of Cantaloupe Island by Herbie Hancock. The name Us3 comes from Us Three, an album by Horace Parlan from 1960, produced by Alfred Lion, the founder of Blue Note Records. The debut album Hand on the Torch is accordingly built on samples from Blue Note tracks that Lion produced.

In 2014 Us3 was dormant, and Wilkinson turned to film music and library music. In 2025 Soundtrack appeared, an album with a cinematic mix of trap rhythms and big band arrangements, with tracks inspired by Gil Evans and Don Ellis. Wilkinson is one of the producers who brought jazz history to a new audience through sampling.
artiest/geoff-wilkinson.listen: Listen to Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia) and notice the sample of Cantaloupe Island by Herbie Hancock and the trumpet of Gerard Presencer. Try to hear what remains of the old jazz track in this new one.

artiest/geoffrey-parsons.text:
Geoffrey Parsons was an Australian pianist who was known above all as an accompanist to singers and instrumentalists. He was born on 15 June 1929 in Summer Hill, a suburb of Sydney, and died on 26 January 1995. He wanted to become an architect, but his love of music won out. From 1941 to 1948 he studied at the New South Wales Conservatorium, and in 1947 he won an ABC competition with Brahms's second piano concerto. In 1950 he travelled to Britain for a tour with the bass-baritone Peter Dawson and stayed on in London.

There he first worked as a pianist in cocktail bars and for five years as accompanist to the duo Anne Ziegler and Webster Booth. A performance of Schubert's Winterreise with Gerhard Hüsch led to his becoming Hüsch's regular accompanist in Munich. In 1961 he played for the first time with Elisabeth Schwarzkopf, at the invitation of Walter Legge, and later became her regular accompanist. He also worked with Victoria de los Ángeles, Nicolai Gedda, Christa Ludwig, Birgit Nilsson and Janet Baker, and later with younger singers such as Thomas Hampson, Olaf Bär and Jessye Norman. His records of Lieder by Schubert and Schumann, including Winterreise from 1989, are among his best known.

After the retirement of Gerald Moore, Parsons was regarded as the best and most sympathetic accompanist of song singers in the world. He gave the role of accompanist new weight through his musicality and quiet strength.
artiest/geoffrey-parsons.listen: Listen to Schubert's Winterreise in Parsons's recording from 1989 and notice how the piano follows the singer and at the same time sets the mood of each song. Try to hear where he gives the singer room.

artiest/georg-friedrich-handel.text: Georg Friedrich Händel came from Halle, learned the craft of opera in Italy and settled in London in 1712. There he wrote dozens of Italian operas, and when the public stayed away from them, he switched to the English-language oratorio. His Messiah had its premiere in Dublin in 1742 and has never left the repertoire since. He wrote the Water Music in 1717 for a boat trip by King George I on the Thames.
artiest/georg-friedrich-handel.listen: Listen to the Alla Hornpipe and hear how horns and trumpets take over the melody from the strings, music made to sound outdoors on the water.

artiest/georg-philipp-telemann.text:
Georg Philipp Telemann was a German Baroque composer and multi-instrumentalist, born in 1681 in Magdeburg and died on 25 June 1767. He is regarded as one of the most prolific composers in history. His father died when he was four. His mother and family forbade him to make music, but he studied in secret and at twelve had already written an opera. He taught himself almost everything. After schools in Magdeburg, Zellerfeld and Hildesheim he went to study law in Leipzig, but chose music after all.

Telemann held important posts in Leipzig, Sorau, Eisenach and Frankfurt before settling in Hamburg in 1721 as music director of the five main churches. His music combines French, Italian and German styles, and Polish folk music sometimes shines through. For organ students he wrote 48 chorale preludes and twenty little fugues. His recordings include suites, concertos for trumpet and works for recorder, viola da gamba and oboe.

His contemporaries counted him among the best German composers. Johann Sebastian Bach made him godfather to his son Carl Philipp Emanuel, and he compared favourably with Bach and Handel, both of whom he knew personally. He always remained at the forefront of new musical currents. His music forms an important link between the late Baroque and the early Classical style. In Hamburg a Telemann museum is dedicated to him.
artiest/georg-philipp-telemann.listen: Listen to a suite by Telemann and see whether you recognise French, Italian or German traits. Telemann blended those styles in his music.

artiest/georg-solti.text:
Sir Georg Solti, born György Stern on 21 October 1912 in Budapest, was a Hungarian-British conductor of orchestras and operas. He died on 5 September 1997. He studied with Béla Bartók, Leó Weiner and Ernő Dohnányi. In the 1930s he was a répétiteur at the Hungarian State Opera and worked for Arturo Toscanini at the Salzburg Festival. Because he was Jewish, he fled in 1938 from the antisemitic laws. He found refuge in Switzerland, where he was not allowed to conduct and earned his living as a pianist.

After the war, in 1946, he became musical director of the Bavarian State Opera in Munich. In 1952 he moved to the opera in Frankfurt, where he stayed for nine years. From 1961 to 1971 he led the opera at Covent Garden in London, which under him received the title Royal Opera. In 1969 he became music director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, a post he held for twenty-two years. He also led the Orchestre de Paris and the London Philharmonic Orchestra.

In his younger years he was known for his intensity; later he was seen as milder. He made more than 250 recordings, including 45 complete operas. Best known is the complete Der Ring des Nibelungen by Wagner for Decca, recorded between 1958 and 1965, of which Das Rheingold appeared in 1959. That recording has twice been declared the best ever made. From 1963 to 1998 he won 31 Grammys, more than anyone else until 2023. He became a British citizen in 1972.
artiest/georg-solti.listen: Listen to the opening of Das Rheingold in Solti's recording from 1959 and notice how the music builds up very slowly. Try to hear how long it takes before a melody emerges.

artiest/george-baker.text:
George Baker is the stage name of Johannes Hans Bouwens, a Dutch singer and songwriter, born on 8 December 1944 in Hoorn. His father, the Italian former soldier Peppino Caruso, had been forced by the Germans to work in the area and was killed in an escape attempt a few months before his birth. Bouwens grew up with his mother and grandparents, from 1957 in Wormerveer. He left school at fourteen and worked unloading ships on the Zaan and later in a lemonade factory. In 1961 he took the pseudonym Body and formed Body and the Wild Cats.

In 1968 he joined the soul band Soul Invention. In the summer of 1969 he wrote Little Green Bag with the bassist Jan Visser. In September 1969 the band recorded a first album and changed its name to George Baker Selection, after a character in a detective novel. Little Green Bag became a worldwide hit, reached number 21 on the Billboard Hot 100 and sold more than a million copies. Only when the second single Dear Ann was also a success did Baker quit his job at the lemonade factory. With his group he scored three international hits: Little Green Bag in 1969, Paloma Blanca in 1975 and Santa Lucia by Night in 1985.

After the group broke up in 1978, Baker performed solo, briefly returned in 1985 with a new Selection and went back to solo projects in 1989. As a solo artist he had released nine albums by 2017.
artiest/george-baker.listen: Listen to Little Green Bag and notice the vocals and the band. The song was written by Baker and Jan Visser in the summer of 1969.

artiest/george-baker-selection.text:
The George Baker Selection was a Dutch pop group from Assendelft. The band began in 1967 as Soul Invention, a soul band that Henk Kramer formed in Assendelft and that played covers of Otis Redding and Sam and Dave. In 1968 Hans Bouwens from Wormerveer joined. In the summer of 1969 he and the bassist Jan Visser wrote Little Green Bag. Because the first recordings were not soul, the group changed its name to The George Baker Selection. Bouwens named himself after a character in a detective novel.

The first album Little Green Bag appeared in 1970 and immediately produced a worldwide hit. In the United States the single reached number 16 on the Cash Box chart and number 21 on the Billboard Hot 100. Baker heard the song on the radio while he was working in a lemonade factory. After the second single Dear Ann he became a full-time musician, and from mid-1970 the group consisted of Baker, Jan Visser, Jan Hop, Jacques Greuter and George Thé. In 1974 the singer Lida Bond joined, and the combination with Baker's voice proved very successful. The fifth album, Paloma Blanca from 1975, contained the single Paloma Blanca, which reached number 1 in several countries.

In 1978 the group broke up because the pressure became too great. In 1982 Baker formed a new Selection, which lasted until 1989. In 1985 the European hit Santa Lucia by Night followed. The band released twelve albums. Baker also wrote for other artists, such as BZN, The Shoes, Andy Star and Next One.
artiest/george-baker-selection.listen: Listen to Paloma Blanca from 1975 and notice how the voice of Lida Bond and that of George Baker sound together. That duo was formed in 1974.

artiest/george-benson.text: The guitarist and singer George Benson from Pittsburgh played as a young musician in Jack McDuff's organ trio and recorded with Miles Davis in 1968. He named Charlie Christian and Wes Montgomery as his models on the guitar. In 1976 he released Breezin', with the vocal hit This Masquerade; the album reached the top of the American albums chart and helped get smooth jazz going. Benson often sings in unison with his own guitar solo. Give Me the Night (1980), produced by Quincy Jones, was a big pop and R&B success.
artiest/george-benson.listen: Hear how the voice and the guitar play exactly the same line at exactly the same time.

artiest/george-chakiris.text:
George Chakiris is an American actor and dancer, born on 16 September 1932 in Norwood, Ohio, the son of Greek immigrants from Turkey. In 1944 the family moved to Long Beach in California. He wanted a career as a dancer and, after a year at Long Beach City College, moved to Hollywood, where he worked in a department store by day and danced in the evenings. He made his film debut in 1947, at fifteen, in the chorus of Song of Love. In the 1950s he had small parts as a dancer in musicals, such as Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, White Christmas and Brigadoon.

His breakthrough came when a close-up with Rosemary Clooney in White Christmas brought in a lot of fan mail, after which Paramount gave him a contract. Around 1958 he went to New York and was given a part in the Broadway musical West Side Story. He is best known as Bernardo, the leader of the Sharks, in the 1961 film version, for which he won an Oscar and a Golden Globe for best supporting actor.

After West Side Story he appeared in Diamond Head and Kings of the Sun, and also began a career as a pop singer with the albums George Chakiris and Memories Are Made of This. Later he worked a great deal in Europe, including in Jacques Demy's The Young Girls of Rochefort. He also appeared in Company on tour and had guest roles in television series such as Hawaii Five-O and Murder, She Wrote. He himself said that many films after West Side Story were a waste of time. His name remains linked above all with Bernardo in West Side Story.
artiest/george-chakiris.listen: Listen to the music of West Side Story, the 1961 film version, and notice how in the scenes with the Sharks dance and song flow into one another. Chakiris plays Bernardo, the leader of the Sharks.

artiest/george-clinton.text:
George Clinton was born on 22 July 1941 in Kannapolis, North Carolina, and grew up in Plainfield, New Jersey. As a teenager he worked in a barbershop, and there he formed The Parliaments, a doo-wop group modelled on Frankie Lymon & the Teenagers. In the 1960s he also worked for a time as a songwriter for Motown. In 1967 The Parliaments had their first big hit with (I Wanna) Testify.

In the 1970s Clinton found his own way with two bands at once: Parliament and Funkadelic. They blended influences from Jimi Hendrix, Sly and the Family Stone, Frank Zappa and James Brown, and experimented with new sounds and technology. With more than forty R&B hits the collective dominated Black music in America for a time. From 1971 to 1973 part of the band lived in Toronto, where America Eats Its Young was made, the first album with the bassist Bootsy Collins. In 1982 Clinton began his solo career with Computer Games, which included Atomic Dog.

Clinton's funk was wilder and stranger than that of his predecessors. He combined heavy grooves with psychedelia, striking costumes, absurd humour and stories about spaceships and the future, a form of Afrofuturism. Together with James Brown and Sly Stone he is regarded as one of the great innovators of funk. When his popularity sank in the 1980s, he came back via hip hop: many rappers cited him as an influence and sampled his music, and the G-funk of the 1990s built on his work. In 1997 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with Parliament-Funkadelic.
artiest/george-clinton.listen: Listen to Atomic Dog (1982). Notice the slow, dragging funk rhythm, the synthesizer bass and the strange, half-barked cries, and hear why so many hip hop producers later sampled this track.
